title: The system: an online shop's order pipeline built on a queue
caption: Checkout only waits for one transaction and one publish; payment, stock and email happen behind the queue, each on its own subscription.

steps.text: A shopper pays. The Checkout API writes the order (status PENDING) and an outbox row in one database transaction and returns 202 with the order id in about 50 ms.
A relay publishes the outbox row as OrderPlaced. The broker stores it durably and acknowledges the publish; the shopper is not waiting for any of this.
Each worker type has its own subscription, so payment, inventory and email each get their own copy and progress independently.
Workers do the side effect with the order id as the idempotency key: charge the card, reserve stock, send the receipt.
A worker acks only after the effect succeeded. On a failure it nacks, and the retry scheduler hands the message back later with backoff and jitter.
After 5 failed attempts the message is parked in the dead-letter queue, so it stops blocking the others. DLQ depth above zero pages someone.

scenarios.name: Flash sale
scenarios.summary: Checkout stays fast at 20× normal traffic: the queue absorbs the burst and the workers drain it at the rate the providers accept.

steps.text: A flash sale brings 20× the usual orders for 15 minutes. The API still only does one transaction and one publish per order.
The backlog grows: orders arrive faster than the payment provider allows (its rate limit caps the worker pool).
Workers keep a steady pace. Inventory and email are faster and finish first; payment lags behind on its own subscription.
The alert to watch is the age of the oldest message, not the depth: a 5-minute-old payment is a support ticket.

scenarios.name: Payment provider down
scenarios.summary: One dependency failing only slows its own subscription; retries with backoff ride out the outage and the DLQ catches what is left.

steps.text: The payment provider returns 503 for 10 minutes.
Each failed charge is nacked and comes back after 1 s, 10 s, then 60 s. Inventory and email are not affected.
Orders that used up 5 attempts during the outage go to the dead-letter queue, and the alert fires.
After the provider recovers, an operator redrives the DLQ into the queue. The idempotency key stops any order from being charged twice.

scenarios.name: Worker deploy
scenarios.summary: A rolling deploy never loses an order: unacked messages simply return to the queue and another worker takes them.

steps.text: A new version of the email worker rolls out, one instance at a time.
A stopping instance finishes and acks what it holds. Anything it had not acked becomes visible again after its timeout.
Another instance receives those messages. A few receipts may be sent twice, so the email step dedupes on order id.
